By Anthony Fenech
Free Press Sports Writer
SAN DIEGO, Calif. — Two winters ago, it was right-hander Michael Fulmer and second baseman Ian Kinsler. Last winter, it was left-hander Matthew Boyd and right fielder Nick Castellanos.
This winter, the Detroit Tigers are nearly out of trade assets.
“Obviously, we’ve made a lot of trades,” general manager Al Avila said this week at the Winter Meetings. “We’ve traded pretty much everybody that we can trade, everybody that we needed to trade.”

A glass-half full view of Avila’s words falls in line with the Tigers’ optimistic message of “Build it back up”: They are past the selling point of their rebuilding, in which every good player seemed to have a shelf life in Detroit before departing for prospects.

A glass-half empty view: They haven’t received nearly enough in trading their batch of All-Star, even elite, players over the past three years - severely limiting the chances for their rebuilding to succeed.
The best perspective likely lies somewhere in the middle, especially considering the recently stagnant trade market the Tigers have tried to operate in, and the contracts they’ve tried to move.

But beginning with Boyd, their 28-year-old left-handed ace, Avila may still have some pieces to work with. And if he wants to expedite what remains a lengthy process, he must try to find incoming or outgoing pieces to pay dividends.

Though Avila professed no intention in moving Boyd earlier in the week, his name continues to pop up on the peripheral of trade rumors, perhaps as a backup plan for teams who miss out on top free agent targets.
“I told these guys, ‘We’re not here calling up every team and saying, ‘Hey, do you want Boyd?’” Avila said. “That’s not what we’re here to do.

“We feel that we want to win some games, we want to win some more games, we want to get better. So, if a team is interested in Matt Boyd - and obviously, there’s teams that will for obvious reasons; pitching right now, everybody needs pitching - so is it going to make the Detroit Tigers better? And when I say, ‘better,’ you’re not getting a prospect that’s in Low A rookie ball, you know what I mean? It’s going to have to really make sense. I’m not out there trying to sell Matt Boyd, so we need Matt Boyd right now to be a good team.”

Boyd went 9-12 with a 4.56 ERA and 1.23 WHIP in 32 starts last season. He showed a strong uptick in swing-and-miss ability, striking out 238 batters in 185 1/3 innings, but struggled mightily in the second half - after likely the peak of his trade value had passed at the July 31 trade deadline - and also led the Major Leagues in home runs allowed.

Still, the Tigers do not appear close to being a good team. And as Boyd gets closer to free agency, Avila must explore the best way to maximize his services. Approaching the trade deadline last season, teams who spoke with the Tigers felt their price on Boyd was too high, asking for cream of the crop prospects, like Brewers top prospect infielder Keston Hiura.

But, looking past Boyd, the Tigers may have a pair of trade possibilities in Niko Goodrum and Jeimer Candelario. Avila said the Tigers have received “a lot” of calls on Goodrum and they have also heard from interested teams on Candelario, according to a person with knowledge of the situation.
Both players, however, may benefit the Tigers more on the field than in a trade — neither figures to garner what the team is looking for in value.
Another option - perhaps less desirable, given the organization’s importance in building their farm system - is trading from their pool of prospects.
Late Tuesday night, MLB Network’s Ken Rosenthal mentioned the Tigers were one of three teams interested in Rangers outfielder Nomar Mazara.
Mazara, 24, is a .261 hitter with 79 home runs and 308 RBI in four seasons, and certainly could have stepped into the middle of the Tigers’ lineup, as it presently shapes up.
The American League Central division-rival White Sox ultimately made the move, sending 2018 second-round pick Steele Walker to Texas.

With a bevy of pitching prospects, perhaps the Tigers could try to bridge their divide in pitching-positional players in such swaps. Or, in the case of Mazara, perhaps they could part with prospects they’ve evaluated as not part of their future for a guy like Mazara who still carries some potential.
Either way, the trade market - and the Tigers’ available players on hand - has given Avila lemons to work with. If he can make lemonade, the Tigers’ rebuilding can receive a boost.
Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press
Tigers beat writer
Twitter: @anthonyfenech
